phy_ocra.18.0.summary: You need to **recall typical speeds** for walking, running, cycling, cars, trains, aircraft, wind and sound, and **typical accelerations** such as free fall and an ordinary car, so you can make sensible estimates. You must also use ratios and proportional reasoning to **convert units** (km/h, mph and m/s; minutes and hours to seconds) and to compute rates such as speed and acceleration. These skills underpin every stopping-distance and road-safety calculation that follows in this topic.

core.p: **Speed** is a rate: it tells you how much distance is covered per unit time. Any rate is found by dividing a quantity by the time taken, so the same proportional reasoning lets you compute speeds, flow rates or energy transfer rates.
bullets: speed (m/s) = distance (m) / time (s)
The SI unit of speed is the **metre per second (m/s)**.
Average speed = total distance / total time taken.
Velocity is speed in a given direction (a vector).
Rate means 'per unit time', e.g. per second or per hour.

callouts.p: The distance travelled per unit time: speed = distance / time.

core.p: OCR expects you to recall approximate values. These are typical figures, so exam answers within a sensible range score.
bullets: Walking about **1.5 m/s**.
Running about **3 m/s** (a sprinter can reach about 10 m/s).
Cycling about **6 m/s**.
Car in town (30 mph) about **13 m/s**; on a motorway (70 mph) about **31 m/s**.
Speeds vary with age, fitness, terrain, distance and slope.

callouts.p: Walk 1.5, run 3, cycle 6, sound in air about 330 m/s.

core.p: The spec names wind and sound specifically. Their speeds are not fixed: they depend on conditions.
bullets: Speed of **sound in air** is about **330 m/s** (depends on temperature).
Sound travels faster in liquids and solids than in air.
**Wind** speed varies a lot: a light breeze is a few m/s, a strong gale more than 20 m/s.
Light travels far faster: 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum, which is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

callouts.p: For echoes, the sound travels there and back, so distance to wall = speed x time / 2.

core.p: Real speeds change during a journey. The value we quote is usually an average.
bullets: A person's walking speed depends on age, fitness, the slope and the surface.
Cars slow at junctions and traffic, so average speed is lower than top speed.
Wind speed changes with weather and height.
Sound speed depends on the material and temperature.

core.p: **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity. It is another rate, so it is a change divided by the time taken.
bullets: acceleration (m/s²) = change in velocity (m/s) / time (s)
a = (v - u) / t where u = starting velocity and v = final velocity.
Units: metres per second squared, **m/s²**.
A negative acceleration is a **deceleration** (slowing down).

callouts.p: The change in velocity per unit time: acceleration = change in velocity / time.

core.p: Knowing typical accelerations helps you judge whether an answer is sensible and estimate forces later in the topic.
bullets: An object in **free fall** near the Earth accelerates at about **10 m/s²** (9.8 m/s²).
A family car accelerating from rest is typically about **2 to 3 m/s²**.
A sprinter leaving the blocks can accelerate at a few m/s².
Accelerations much bigger than g (10 m/s²) are rare in everyday life except in collisions.

callouts.p: If you calculate a car's acceleration as 300 m/s², something has gone wrong (probably km/h not converted).

core.p: On a velocity-time graph, the **gradient** is the acceleration. A straight sloping line means constant acceleration; a horizontal line means constant speed.
bullets: gradient = change in velocity / change in time = acceleration
Steeper line = greater acceleration.
Downward slope = deceleration.
Area under the line = distance travelled (useful in later points).

core.p: Calculations need SI units (m/s), but road speeds are given in mph or km/h. Use ratios: there are 1000 m in a km and 3600 s in an hour.
bullets: km/h to m/s: multiply by 1000, divide by 3600, i.e. **divide by 3.6**.
m/s to km/h: **multiply by 3.6**.
1 mile is about 1600 m, so 1 mph is about 0.45 m/s.
mph to m/s: multiply by about 0.45; m/s to mph: multiply by about 2.24.
Example: 72 km/h / 3.6 = 20 m/s.

callouts.p: Write 72 km/h = 72 000 m per 3600 s = 20 m/s. Method marks reward the conversion step.

core.p: Before using an equation, convert every quantity to base SI units: metres, seconds, kilograms.
bullets: 1 minute = 60 s; 1 hour = 60 minutes = 3600 s.
1 mile is about 1.6 km (1600 m).
Reaction times are often in milliseconds: 1 ms = 0.001 s.

core.p: Proportional reasoning means scaling quantities using a ratio. If speed is constant, distance is directly proportional to time: double the time, double the distance.
bullets: At 6 m/s, a cyclist travels 6 m every second, so 360 m every minute.
To find time: time = distance / speed.
Use unit ratios as fractions equal to 1, e.g. (1000 m / 1 km) or (1 h / 3600 s).
Check whether the answer should be bigger or smaller after converting.

core.p: Exam questions often say 'estimate'. You must choose a sensible typical value yourself, state it, and use it.
bullets: Example: estimate time to walk 1.2 km: 1200 / 1.5 = 800 s (about 13 minutes).
Round to 1 or 2 significant figures; an estimate should not be over-precise.
State your assumption, e.g. 'assume walking speed is 1.5 m/s'.

callouts.p: Write your assumed value clearly; examiners accept a range (e.g. 1 to 2 m/s for walking).

core.p: Most errors in this topic come from units rather than physics.
bullets: Convert to m and s first, then substitute into the equation.
Write units on every line of working.
Compare your answer with typical values: is it reasonable?
Give acceleration in m/s² and speed in m/s unless asked otherwise.

analogy.p: Converting units is like changing money abroad. 1 m/s is worth 3.6 km/h, just as 1 pound might buy a fixed number of euros. You multiply or divide by the exchange rate, and the actual amount (how fast you are going, or how much money you have) does not change, only the units used to describe it. Where it breaks down: currency rates change from day to day and banks take a fee, whereas unit conversion factors are fixed and exact (apart from rounding).

terms.d: Distance travelled per unit time; a scalar.
Speed in a given direction; a vector.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
Rate of change of velocity: change in velocity / time.
Negative acceleration; slowing down.
Metres per second, the SI unit of speed.
Metres per second squared, the SI unit of acceleration.
Acceleration of a falling object near Earth with no air resistance, about 10 m/s².
How much a quantity changes per unit time.
A comparison of two quantities, used to scale or convert units.
Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other.
Changing a quantity into different units without changing its size.
An approximate value found using sensible typical values and rounding.
Change in y divided by change in x; on a velocity-time graph it gives acceleration.
About 330 m/s in air; higher in liquids and solids.

mistakes.w: Dividing km/h by 60 to get m/s.
mistakes.r: Divide by 3.6 (1000 m per km and 3600 s per hour).

mistakes.w: Using a time in minutes or hours in v = d / t.
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds first.

mistakes.w: Typical walking speed is 15 m/s.
mistakes.r: Walking is about 1.5 m/s.

mistakes.w: Speed of sound is 3 x 10^8 m/s.
mistakes.r: That is light; sound in air is about 330 m/s.

mistakes.w: Acceleration in m/s.
mistakes.r: Acceleration is in m/s².

mistakes.w: Acceleration = velocity / time using final velocity only, when the object did not start from rest.
mistakes.r: Use change in velocity: (v - u) / t.

mistakes.w: Giving an estimate to 5 significant figures.
mistakes.r: Estimates should be rounded to 1 or 2 significant figures with the assumption stated.

mistakes.w: Multiplying by 3.6 when converting km/h to m/s.
mistakes.r: Speeds in m/s are smaller numbers than in km/h, so divide by 3.6.

steps: Light arrives almost instantly, so the delay is the time for sound.

phy_ocra.18.1.summary: **Reaction time** is the time between a person detecting a stimulus (seeing or hearing something) and responding to it; for most people it is typically **0.2 s to 0.9 s**. OCR expects you to explain methods of measuring it, especially the **ruler drop test** (and electronic or computer timers), to convert a drop distance into a time, to plan a fair and repeatable investigation, and to explain how factors such as tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions increase reaction time and so affect driving safety.

core.p: Reaction time is how long it takes you to **respond to a stimulus**. Your sense organs detect the stimulus, nerves carry signals to the brain, the brain decides what to do, and nerves carry signals to the muscles. All of this takes time.
bullets: Measured in seconds (often quoted in milliseconds, ms).
Typical human reaction time is **0.2 s to 0.9 s**.
It varies from person to person and for the same person at different times.
A longer reaction time means a longer **thinking distance** when driving.

callouts.p: The time between a stimulus occurring and a person responding to it.

core.p: The ruler drop test is a simple way to measure reaction time in the lab. The faster you react, the less distance the ruler falls before you catch it.
bullets: Person A holds a metre ruler (or 30 cm ruler) vertically, with the **zero mark** level with person B's open thumb and finger.
Person B rests their arm on the edge of a table so their hand is steady.
Without warning, person A **drops** the ruler.
Person B catches it as quickly as possible.
Read the distance fallen at the **top of the thumb** (where it is caught).
Repeat several times and calculate a mean distance.
Convert the distance to a reaction time using a conversion table, graph or equation.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward: start at zero, no warning, read where caught, repeat and average, convert distance to time.

core.h: Why the distance tells you the time
core.p: When dropped, the ruler accelerates downwards at **g = 10 m/s²** (approx.), starting from rest. The longer you take to react, the faster it is moving and the further it falls. Because it is speeding up, distance is **not proportional** to time: doubling the time makes it fall four times as far.
bullets: The ruler starts from rest (u = 0) and accelerates uniformly at g.
Using v² = u² + 2 a s: final speed of ruler v = square root of (2 g d).
Using a = (v - u) / t: time t = v / g.
Combining gives **t = square root of (2d / g)**, with d in metres.
Air resistance on a ruler is small, so it can be ignored.

callouts.p: d = 0.5 x g x t² so t = square root of (2d / g). With g = 10 m/s², a 0.20 m drop gives t = 0.20 s.

bullets: Read the drop distance, then look up the time.

A 30 cm ruler can only measure reaction times up to about 0.25 s.

callouts.p: If reaction times are longer than about 0.25 s, a 30 cm ruler hits the floor before it is caught: use a metre ruler.

core.p: To compare reaction times (for example with and without a distraction) you must control other variables.
bullets: Use the **same ruler** and the same starting position (zero level with fingers).
Use the **same hand** (dominant hand) each time.
Same gap between thumb and finger.
Same person dropping, with no warning or countdown.
Arm resting on the table edge so only the fingers move.

head: Variable type
Example
rows: Distraction or not / hand used / time of day
Same ruler, same hand, same gap, same dropper, no warning

core.p: Single measurements vary a lot, so repeats are essential.
bullets: Repeat at least 5 times and calculate the **mean**.
Identify and discard **anomalous** results (e.g. if the catcher anticipated the drop).
Vary the time before dropping randomly so the catcher cannot predict it.
Read the scale at eye level to avoid parallax error.
The ruler's resolution (1 mm) is small compared with typical drop distances, so reading error is small.

callouts.p: Variation between repeats is random error; averaging repeats reduces its effect.

core.p: Reaction time can also be measured with an electronic timer or a computer program: a light comes on (or a sound plays) and the timer stops when the person presses a button.
bullets: Timer starts automatically when the stimulus appears.
Timer stops when the button is pressed.
Gives times to the nearest millisecond, with no human reading error.
Easy to repeat many times and calculate a mean.
The response is a button press, which may not match real tasks like braking.

Advantage
Disadvantage

core.p: Anything that slows the brain processing or the nerve signals increases reaction time.
bullets: **Tiredness**: the brain processes information more slowly.
**Alcohol** and many **drugs** (including some medicines) slow down the nervous system.
**Distractions** such as using a mobile phone, talking or loud music divert attention.
**Age**: reaction times tend to be longer in older people.
Illness and poor concentration also increase reaction time.

callouts.p: Tiredness, alcohol and distractions affect reaction time (thinking distance), not the car's brakes.

core.h: Why reaction time matters for driving
core.p: During the reaction time, a vehicle keeps moving at the same speed. The distance travelled in this time is the **thinking distance**, so a longer reaction time or a higher speed both increase it.
bullets: thinking distance = speed x reaction time
At 13 m/s with a 0.7 s reaction time, thinking distance is about 9 m.
Doubling reaction time doubles thinking distance.
This is why drink-driving and using a phone while driving are dangerous.

core.p: Reaction time can be measured for different stimuli: seeing (visual), hearing (auditory) or touch. A fair comparison changes only the stimulus.
bullets: Ruler drop uses a visual stimulus (seeing the ruler move).
A computer test can use a light, a sound or both.
Expect people to improve with practice, so practise first or randomise the order.

core.p: Present results in a table with repeats and a mean, then convert to reaction times. Use a bar chart to compare conditions (categoric independent variable).
bullets: Calculate mean drop distance, ignoring anomalies.
Convert the mean distance to a time (do not average the times and distances inconsistently).
Range of repeats shows how repeatable results are.
Draw conclusions only if the difference between conditions is bigger than the spread.

core.p: Questions on this point are often 'describe a method' or 'evaluate a method' plus a short calculation.
bullets: Use the words stimulus, response, repeat, mean, anomalous, control variable.
Quote typical values: 0.2 to 0.9 s.
Show the conversion: d in metres, t = square root of (2d / g).
Link any factor to a longer reaction time and then a longer thinking distance.

analogy.t: A relay team passing a message
analogy.p: Reaction time is like a relay race inside your body: your eyes spot the signal and pass the baton along nerves to your brain, which decides and passes it to your muscles. The total race time is your reaction time. Tiredness or alcohol is like runners jogging instead of sprinting, so the baton arrives later. Where it breaks down: in a relay each runner covers a set distance one after another, whereas nerve signals travel very fast and most of the delay is the brain processing and deciding, not the travel itself.

phy_ocra.18.2.summary: The **stopping distance** of a vehicle is the total distance it travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment it stops: **stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance**. **Thinking distance** depends on the vehicle's speed and the driver's **reaction time**, which is made longer by tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions. **Braking distance** depends on speed, the vehicle's mass and the friction available from the brakes, tyres and road surface, which is reduced by worn brakes, worn tyres and wet or icy roads. Speed matters most because thinking distance is proportional to speed but braking distance is proportional to speed squared.

core.p: When a driver spots a hazard the car does not stop instantly. First the car keeps moving at a steady speed while the driver reacts, then it slows down while the brakes act. The two distances add together.
bullets: **Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance**
**Thinking distance**: distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied
**Braking distance**: distance travelled after the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops
During thinking distance the speed is constant (no braking force yet)
During braking distance the vehicle decelerates
Any factor that increases either part increases the overall stopping distance

callouts.p: The sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.
The distance a vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time, between seeing a hazard and applying the brakes.
The distance a vehicle travels after the brakes are applied until it comes to a stop.

core.p: Reaction time is the time between the driver seeing a hazard and their foot pressing the brake. Nerve signals must travel from the eyes to the brain, a decision is made, then signals go to the leg muscles. A typical reaction time is about 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
bullets: Typical reaction time is roughly **0.2 to 0.9 s**
Longer reaction time means the car travels further at full speed before braking starts
Reaction time affects **thinking distance only**, not braking distance
Reaction time varies from person to person and from moment to moment

callouts.p: The time taken for a person to respond to a stimulus, such as the time between seeing a hazard and applying the brakes.

core.p: Because the car travels at a constant speed during the reaction time, thinking distance is found with the normal speed equation.
bullets: **thinking distance = speed x reaction time** (distance = speed x time)
Units: m = m/s x s
Example: 20 m/s x 0.7 s = 14 m
Thinking distance is **directly proportional to speed** if reaction time is constant
Doubling speed **doubles** thinking distance
Doubling reaction time also **doubles** thinking distance

callouts.p: Speeds given in km/h or mph must be converted to m/s before using distance = speed x time to get an answer in metres.

core.p: Anything that slows down the driver's reactions, or makes the car faster, increases thinking distance.
bullets: **Speed**: higher speed means more metres covered every second of reaction time
**Tiredness**: a tired driver reacts more slowly
**Alcohol**: a depressant that slows the nervous system and increases reaction time
**Drugs**: some illegal and some prescription or over-the-counter medicines increase reaction time
**Distractions**: using a mobile phone, talking to passengers, adjusting the radio or sat nav
**Age and inexperience** can affect how quickly a driver recognises a hazard
Poor visibility (fog, darkness) can delay noticing the hazard

callouts.p: A wet or icy road does NOT change thinking distance. It affects braking distance only.

core.p: When the driver presses the brake pedal, brake pads are pushed against a disc attached to the wheel. Friction between the pads and the disc produces a braking force that opposes the motion. Work is done by this friction force, transferring energy from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes.
bullets: Friction between **brake pads and brake disc** slows the wheels
Friction between **tyres and road** slows the car itself
Work done by the brakes = braking force x braking distance
Energy is transferred from the **kinetic energy store** to the **thermal energy store** of the brakes (and surroundings)
The brakes get hot; very hard braking can make them overheat and become less effective
Kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed²

callouts.p: braking force x braking distance = kinetic energy = 0.5 x m x v². So braking distance = 0.5 x m x v² / F.

core.p: Braking distance increases if the car has more kinetic energy to get rid of, or if the maximum braking (friction) force is smaller.
bullets: **Speed**: more speed means much more kinetic energy (KE ∝ v²)
**Mass of vehicle**: a heavily loaded car or lorry has more kinetic energy at the same speed
**Condition of brakes**: worn brakes give a smaller friction force
**Condition of tyres**: worn tyres with little tread grip the road less
**Road surface**: wet, icy, oily, gravel or leaf-covered roads reduce friction between tyres and road
**Weather**: rain, ice and snow all reduce grip
Downhill slopes also increase braking distance

Why it increases braking distance
rows: More kinetic energy to transfer, KE ∝ v²
More kinetic energy at the same speed
Smaller friction force from the brakes
Less grip, smaller maximum friction with road
Less friction between tyres and road

core.h: Why speed has the biggest effect on braking distance
core.p: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. If the braking force stays the same, the work done (force x distance) needed to stop the car must equal the kinetic energy, so the braking distance is proportional to speed squared.
bullets: F x d = 0.5 x m x v², so **d ∝ v²** when F and m are constant
**Doubling speed** gives **4 times** the kinetic energy, so **4 times** the braking distance
**Tripling speed** gives **9 times** the braking distance
Thinking distance only doubles when speed doubles
So at high speed, braking distance becomes the larger part of stopping distance

callouts.p: Thinking distance ∝ speed. Braking distance ∝ speed². Doubling speed doubles thinking distance and quadruples braking distance.

core.p: The tyres must grip the road for the braking force to slow the car. The maximum friction between tyre and road limits how hard the car can brake without skidding.
bullets: Tyre **tread** channels water away so the rubber stays in contact with the road
Worn tread on a wet road can cause **aquaplaning**: a layer of water lifts the tyre off the road
The UK legal minimum tread depth for cars is 1.6 mm
If the braking force is greater than the maximum friction, the wheels **lock** and the car **skids**
A skidding car has less control and usually a longer braking distance
Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) stop the wheels locking

callouts.p: On ice, the friction between tyres and road is very small, so braking distance can be many times longer than on a dry road.

core.p: A heavier vehicle travelling at the same speed has more kinetic energy. With the same braking force, it needs a longer distance to transfer all that energy.
bullets: KE = 0.5 x m x v², so doubling mass doubles kinetic energy
With the same braking force, **braking distance ∝ mass**
Also: deceleration = force / mass, so a larger mass gives a smaller deceleration
Lorries, buses and loaded cars need longer braking distances
Mass does NOT affect thinking distance

core.p: The Highway Code gives typical stopping distances on a dry road for an alert driver in a car with good brakes and tyres. They show how braking distance grows much faster than thinking distance.
bullets: 20 mph (about 9 m/s): thinking 6 m, braking 6 m, stopping 12 m
30 mph (about 13 m/s): thinking 9 m, braking 14 m, stopping 23 m
50 mph (about 22 m/s): thinking 15 m, braking 38 m, stopping 53 m
70 mph (about 31 m/s): thinking 21 m, braking 75 m, stopping 96 m
Wet roads can roughly double braking distance; icy roads can increase it up to about ten times

callouts.p: Check the table: thinking distance at 70 mph is about 3.5 times that at 20 mph (speed ratio 3.5), but braking distance is about 12 times (3.5² ≈ 12).

core.p: Understanding the factors explains road safety laws and advice.
bullets: **Speed limits** are lower near schools and in towns because stopping distance falls sharply at lower speeds
**Drink-drive and drug-drive laws** reduce reaction time problems
Banning hand-held **mobile phones** while driving reduces distractions
Keep a safe **following distance** (two-second rule; double it in the wet)
Drive more slowly in rain, fog, ice or snow
Keep brakes and tyres maintained; check tread depth

callouts.p: Separate your answer into thinking distance factors and braking distance factors, give the effect of each and explain WHY using reaction time, friction or kinetic energy.

analogy.p: Stopping is like a relay race with two runners. The first runner (your brain) must react before passing the baton; while it hesitates the car keeps moving at full speed, so a slow first runner (tired, drunk or distracted driver) adds thinking distance. The second runner (brakes and tyres) then has to 'carry away' all the kinetic energy; a weak second runner (worn brakes, icy road) or a heavier load (more speed or mass) means a longer leg. Where it breaks down: in a relay both runners run at similar speeds, but in a car the second leg grows with speed squared while the first only grows in proportion to speed.

terms.d: Thinking distance plus braking distance; the total distance travelled from seeing a hazard to stopping.
Distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, at constant speed, before the brakes are applied.
Distance travelled from when the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops.
Time between a stimulus (seeing a hazard) and the response (applying the brakes); typically 0.2 to 0.9 s.
A force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact.
The friction force from the brakes (and between tyres and road) that decelerates the vehicle.
Energy in the kinetic store of a moving object; KE = 0.5 x m x v².
Energy transferred when a force moves through a distance; work done = force x distance.
Negative acceleration; the rate at which speed decreases.
The grooves on a tyre that push water away so the tyre keeps gripping the road.
When a layer of water builds up between tyre and road so the tyre loses contact and grip.
Sliding of a vehicle when the braking force needed is greater than the maximum friction between tyres and road.
When one quantity doubles, the other doubles; thinking distance is directly proportional to speed.
The store energy is transferred to when brakes heat up during braking.

mistakes.w: A wet road increases thinking distance.
mistakes.r: A wet road reduces friction so increases braking distance only; thinking distance is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Alcohol increases braking distance.
mistakes.r: Alcohol increases reaction time, so it increases thinking distance (and therefore stopping distance), not braking distance.

mistakes.w: Doubling speed doubles the braking distance.
mistakes.r: Braking distance ∝ speed², so doubling speed quadruples braking distance.

mistakes.w: Stopping distance = thinking distance x braking distance.
mistakes.r: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

mistakes.w: Tiredness makes the brakes work slower.
mistakes.r: Tiredness increases the driver's reaction time, increasing thinking distance.

mistakes.w: Worn tyres increase reaction time.
mistakes.r: Worn tyres reduce grip/friction with the road, increasing braking distance.

mistakes.w: Brakes turn kinetic energy into heat (with no mention of work or stores).
mistakes.r: Work done by the friction force transfers energy from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes.

mistakes.w: Mass affects thinking distance.
mistakes.r: Mass only affects braking distance; thinking distance depends on speed and reaction time.

mistakes.w: Ice makes the car go faster so it stops later.
mistakes.r: Ice reduces friction between the tyres and road so the maximum braking force is smaller and braking distance increases.

exam.q: State the equation that links stopping distance, thinking distance and braking distance.
model: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
exam.tip: Words or symbols both get the mark; never multiply.

exam.q: Give two factors that increase the thinking distance of a car.
model: Any two from: higher speed; tiredness; alcohol; drugs; distractions such as using a mobile phone
exam.tip: Do not give road or tyre conditions; they affect braking distance.

exam.q: Give two factors that increase the braking distance of a car.
model: Any two from: higher speed; greater mass; worn brakes; worn tyres; wet or icy road surface
exam.tip: 'Bad weather' alone may not score; say 'wet or icy road'.

exam.q: A driver has a reaction time of 0.6 s and is travelling at 25 m/s. Calculate the thinking distance.
model: thinking distance = speed x reaction time = 25 x 0.6
exam.tip: Always show the equation, then substitution.

exam.q: Explain why driving after drinking alcohol increases the stopping distance of a car.
model: Alcohol increases the driver's reaction time
so the car travels further before the brakes are applied, increasing thinking distance (and stopping distance)
exam.tip: Link the factor to reaction time, then to thinking distance.

exam.q: Explain why a wet road increases the stopping distance of a car.
model: Less friction (grip) between the tyres and the road
so a smaller braking force, giving a longer braking distance
exam.tip: Name the two surfaces: tyres and road.

exam.q: The braking distance of a car at 15 m/s is 18 m. Predict the braking distance at 30 m/s, assuming the braking force is the same. Explain your answer.
model: Braking distance is proportional to speed squared
Speed doubles so braking distance is multiplied by 4
Braking distance = 72 m
exam.tip: Use the ratio rule rather than recalculating from scratch.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfer when a car brakes to a stop.
model: Work is done by the friction force between the brake pads and discs
Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes/surroundings
exam.tip: Use the word 'store' and mention work done by friction.

exam.q: Explain why a loaded van has a longer braking distance than the same empty van at the same speed.
model: The loaded van has more mass so more kinetic energy (KE = 0.5mv²)
With the same braking force, more work is needed so it travels further while braking (or smaller deceleration, a = F/m)
exam.tip: Either the energy argument or the F = ma argument scores.

exam.q: Describe and explain the factors that affect the stopping distance of a car. [6 marks]
model: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
Thinking distance increases with speed (distance = speed x reaction time)
Thinking distance increases with longer reaction time caused by tiredness, alcohol, drugs or distractions
Braking distance increases with speed, proportional to speed squared because KE = 0.5mv²
Braking distance increases with greater mass because there is more kinetic energy to transfer
Braking distance increases with worn brakes or tyres or wet/icy roads because there is less friction so a smaller braking force
exam.tip: Level 3 answers cover BOTH parts of stopping distance with clear explanations of why.

worked.q: A car travels at 18 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.5 s. The braking distance is 24 m. Calculate the stopping distance. The driver then becomes tired and their reaction time increases to 0.9 s. Calculate the new stopping distance.
steps: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time = 18 x 0.5 = 9 m
Braking distance is unchanged (tiredness does not affect the brakes or road) = 24 m
worked.ans: 33 m when alert; 40.2 m when tired

worked.q: At 10 m/s a car's thinking distance is 7 m and braking distance is 6 m. Estimate the stopping distance at 30 m/s with the same driver and road.
steps: Speed increases by a factor of 3
Braking distance ∝ speed²: 6 x 3² = 6 x 9 = 54 m
worked.ans: 75 m (the braking distance has grown 9 times while the thinking distance only tripled)

worked.q: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes with a constant braking force of 6000 N. Calculate the braking distance.
steps: Kinetic energy = 0.5 x m x v² = 0.5 x 1200 x 20² = 240 000 J
Work done by brakes = kinetic energy, so F x d = 240 000

phy_ocra.18.3.summary: Triple students must be able to **estimate** how far a vehicle travels before stopping from a hazard at typical road speeds. You choose sensible values (speed, a reaction time of about 0.7 s, and a braking deceleration of roughly 6 to 7 m/s² on a dry road), then work out **thinking distance = speed x reaction time** and **braking distance from v² - u² = 2as**, and add them. Typical answers are about 12 m at 20 mph, about 23 m at 30 mph and about 96 m at 70 mph, showing that stopping distance grows much faster than speed.

core.p: An estimate is a calculation done with sensible, rounded typical values rather than exact measured ones. Exam questions often say 'estimate' and expect you to choose the values yourself, then show the working clearly.
bullets: Use **typical values** you are expected to know (speeds, reaction time, deceleration, masses)
Round to 1 or 2 significant figures; the answer is approximate
State the values you have assumed
An answer in the right **order of magnitude** (tens of metres for a car) is what matters
Your final answer should be sensible: a car at 30 mph does not need 500 m to stop

callouts.p: Write 'Assume reaction time = 0.7 s' so the examiner can award method marks even if your value differs from theirs.

core.p: You need typical speeds in m/s, because the equations use SI units.
bullets: Walking: about **1.5 m/s**
Cycling: about **6 m/s**
Car in a town (30 mph): about **13 m/s**
Car on a main road (50 mph): about **22 m/s**
Car on a motorway (70 mph): about **31 m/s**
1 mph ≈ 0.45 m/s; to change km/h to m/s divide by 3.6

callouts.p: Using 30 instead of 13 m/s for a 30 mph car gives an answer more than twice too big. Always convert to m/s first.

core.p: Reaction time is the delay between seeing the hazard and pressing the brake. For an alert driver it is usually somewhere between about 0.2 s and 0.9 s; 0.7 s is a sensible value to use in estimates.
bullets: Typical range: **0.2 to 0.9 s**
Sensible estimate: **about 0.7 s** (the Highway Code figures correspond to about 0.67 s)
A tired, drunk or distracted driver may take well over 1 s
A longer reaction time increases **thinking distance** in proportion

core.p: During the reaction time the car does not slow down, so thinking distance comes straight from distance = speed x time.
bullets: **thinking distance = speed x reaction time**
Thinking distance is **directly proportional to speed**

callouts.p: Thinking distance is calculated at constant speed because the brakes have not yet been applied.

core.p: A car with good brakes and tyres on a dry road can decelerate at roughly 6 to 7 m/s². The Highway Code braking distances correspond to about 6.5 m/s². Wet or icy roads give much smaller decelerations.
bullets: Dry road, good car: about **6 to 7 m/s²**
Wet road: deceleration can roughly halve, so braking distance roughly doubles
Icy road: deceleration can be around a tenth, so braking distance up to about ten times
Emergency braking decelerations greater than about 10 m/s² are not reached by normal cars because tyre friction limits them

callouts.p: If you put a = -6.5 m/s² into v² - u² = 2as, keep the minus sign consistently; or use the magnitude in d = u² / 2a.

core.h: Estimating braking distance with v² - u² = 2as
core.p: Braking is (approximately) uniform deceleration, so the equation of motion from the data sheet can be used. The final speed v is 0.
bullets: **(final velocity)² - (initial velocity)² = 2 x acceleration x distance**
With v = 0: 0 - u² = 2 x (-a) x d, so **d = u² / (2a)**
Because d ∝ u², doubling speed gives 4 times the braking distance

callouts.p: v² - u² = 2as is given on the OCR equation sheet; you must be able to rearrange it for distance.

core.p: An alternative is to use work done. The braking force does work equal to the car's kinetic energy.
bullets: braking force x braking distance = 0.5 x m x v²
d = 0.5 x m x v² / F
Example: 1000 kg car, 13 m/s, braking force 6500 N: d = 0.5 x 1000 x 169 / 6500 ≈ 13 m
This agrees with the v² - u² = 2as method because F = ma

core.h: Putting it together: the estimation method
core.p: Follow the same four steps every time.
bullets: Step 1: choose or convert a **typical speed** in m/s
Step 2: **thinking distance** = speed x reaction time (about 0.7 s)
Step 3: **braking distance** = speed² / (2 x deceleration) (about 6.5 m/s²)
Step 4: **stopping distance** = thinking + braking
Check the answer is sensible against the Highway Code values

core.p: Stopping distance can also be found from a velocity-time graph: the area under the graph equals the distance travelled.
bullets: Flat section = reaction time; area of the **rectangle** = thinking distance
Sloping section = braking; area of the **triangle** = braking distance = 0.5 x base x height
Gradient of the sloping line = deceleration
Total area = stopping distance
A longer reaction time makes the rectangle wider; a slippery road makes the slope less steep and the triangle longer

core.p: Converting metres into car lengths helps you check whether an estimate is sensible and explains why keeping a safe gap matters.
bullets: Car length ≈ 4 m, so divide stopping distance by 4
30 mph ≈ 6 car lengths; 70 mph ≈ 24 car lengths
A football pitch is about 100 m long, roughly the stopping distance at 70 mph
The two-second rule gives a gap of 2 x speed; at 31 m/s that is about 62 m, enough because the car ahead also needs distance to stop

fig.cap: At 30 mph a car needs about 23 m to stop, roughly six car lengths; at 70 mph it needs about 96 m, roughly 24 car lengths.

core.h: Effect of changing conditions on estimates
core.p: Estimates can be adapted to different conditions by changing the reaction time or the deceleration.
bullets: Tired driver (reaction time 1.4 s instead of 0.7 s): thinking distance **doubles**
Wet road (deceleration halved): braking distance **doubles**
Icy road: braking distance up to about **10 times** larger
Faster speed: thinking distance x speed factor, braking distance x (speed factor)²
Heavier vehicle with the same braking force: smaller deceleration, longer braking distance

callouts.p: If a question gives one stopping distance, use ratios to scale to a new speed rather than starting again.

analogy.p: Imagine sprinting towards a wall with your eyes on a friend who shouts 'stop'. You keep running for a moment while you react (thinking distance, fixed time, so faster running covers more ground) and then you skid to a halt (braking distance). Estimating is like guessing how many paces you need: use your usual reaction time and how hard your shoes can grip. Where it breaks down: a person can stop much more quickly relative to their speed than a car, and a car's braking distance depends on tyre and road friction, not leg strength.

terms.d: An approximate value worked out using sensible typical values and rounding.
A sensible everyday value, e.g. walking 1.5 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, car 13 to 31 m/s.
Time between seeing a hazard and applying the brakes; typically 0.2 to 0.9 s, about 0.7 s for estimates.
Distance travelled during the reaction time; speed x reaction time.
Distance travelled while the brakes slow the vehicle to rest; u² / 2a for uniform deceleration.
Thinking distance + braking distance.
Rate of decrease of velocity, in m/s²; typically about 6 to 7 m/s² for a car braking on a dry road.
Deceleration that stays constant, so velocity falls by the same amount each second.
Equation of motion linking final velocity, initial velocity, acceleration and distance for uniform acceleration.
Equals the distance travelled.
Equals the acceleration (negative for deceleration).
The size of a number to the nearest power of ten; used to judge whether an estimate is sensible.
Force x distance; the work done by the brakes equals the kinetic energy removed.
UK rules of the road giving typical stopping distances, e.g. 23 m at 30 mph and 96 m at 70 mph.

mistakes.w: Using the speed in mph directly in distance = speed x time.
mistakes.r: Convert to m/s first (30 mph ≈ 13 m/s) to get a distance in metres.

mistakes.w: Braking distance = speed x braking time.
mistakes.r: The speed is falling during braking: use v² - u² = 2as, or 0.5 x speed x time (area of triangle).

mistakes.w: Doubling speed doubles stopping distance.
mistakes.r: Thinking distance doubles but braking distance quadruples, so stopping distance more than doubles.

mistakes.w: Choosing a reaction time of 5 s or 0.01 s.
mistakes.r: Use a sensible value of about 0.2 to 0.9 s (0.7 s is ideal).

mistakes.w: Forgetting the 0.5 when finding the area of the braking triangle.
mistakes.r: Braking distance = 0.5 x base x height on a v-t graph.

mistakes.w: Giving only braking distance when asked for stopping distance.
mistakes.r: Stopping distance = thinking + braking; add both parts.

mistakes.w: Putting v = initial speed and u = 0 in v² - u² = 2as.
mistakes.r: u is the initial speed, v = 0 is the final speed; the deceleration is negative.

mistakes.w: Stating an estimate with many significant figures, e.g. 22.0769 m.
mistakes.r: Round sensibly, e.g. about 22 m, because the input values are only approximate.

exam.q: State a typical value for the reaction time of an alert driver.
model: Any value from 0.2 s to 0.9 s (e.g. 0.7 s)

exam.q: Give a typical speed in m/s for a car travelling in a town.
model: About 13 m/s (accept 10 to 15 m/s)

exam.q: A car travels at 13 m/s. Estimate its thinking distance.
model: Sensible reaction time chosen, e.g. 0.7 s
Thinking distance = 13 x 0.7 ≈ 9 m

exam.q: A car travelling at 20 m/s decelerates uniformly at 6.5 m/s². Calculate its braking distance.
model: v² - u² = 2as with v = 0
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting to avoid sign errors.

exam.q: Estimate the stopping distance of a car on a motorway.
model: Typical speed about 31 m/s (70 mph)
Thinking distance = 31 x 0.7 ≈ 22 m
Braking distance = 31² / (2 x 6.5) ≈ 74 m
Stopping distance ≈ 96 m (accept 70 to 120 m with working)
exam.tip: Four marks: one for each assumed value or stage and one for the total.

exam.q: A v-t graph shows a car at 15 m/s for 0.6 s, then slowing uniformly to rest in 2.5 s. Calculate the stopping distance.
model: Thinking distance = 15 x 0.6 = 9 m
Braking distance = 0.5 x 2.5 x 15 = 18.75 m
Stopping distance ≈ 27.75 m (28 m)

exam.q: The stopping distance at 30 mph is about 23 m, of which 9 m is thinking distance. Estimate the stopping distance at 60 mph.
model: Thinking distance doubles to 18 m
Braking distance (14 m) x 4 = 56 m
Stopping distance ≈ 74 m
exam.tip: Split into the two parts before scaling.

exam.q: Explain why the stopping distance on a wet road is longer, and estimate the braking distance at 13 m/s if the deceleration falls to 3.2 m/s².
model: Less friction between tyres and road
so smaller braking force and smaller deceleration
Braking distance = 13² / (2 x 3.2)

exam.q: A student estimates the stopping distance of a car at 30 mph as 600 m. Explain why this is not sensible and identify a likely error.
model: Typical stopping distance at 30 mph is about 23 m (a few car lengths), so 600 m is far too large
Likely used speed in mph (30) or km/h instead of m/s, or omitted the 2 in v²/2a / mixed units

exam.q: Describe how you would estimate the stopping distance of a car travelling at a typical town speed. Include any values you would use. [6 marks]
model: Choose typical speed, about 13 m/s (30 mph)
Choose typical reaction time about 0.7 s
Thinking distance = speed x reaction time ≈ 9 m
Choose typical deceleration about 6.5 m/s² on a dry road
Braking distance from v² - u² = 2as, d = u² / 2a ≈ 13 m
Stopping distance = thinking + braking ≈ 22 m; state it depends on driver and road conditions
exam.tip: A full answer gives values, equations and the final estimate.

worked.q: Estimate the stopping distance of a car travelling at 30 mph on a dry road.
steps: Assume reaction time = 0.7 s: thinking distance = 13 x 0.7 = 9.1 m
Braking distance: 0 - 13² = 2 x (-6.5) x s, so s = 169 / 13 = 13 m
worked.ans: About 22 m (close to the Highway Code value of 23 m)

worked.q: Estimate the stopping distance of a car travelling at 70 mph (31 m/s) on a dry road, and then on a wet road where the deceleration is halved.
steps: Wet: deceleration = 3.25 m/s², braking distance = 961 / 6.5 ≈ 148 m
worked.ans: About 96 m dry; about 170 m wet (braking distance doubles, thinking distance unchanged)

worked.q: A cyclist travels at 6 m/s, has a reaction time of 0.5 s and can decelerate at 4 m/s². Estimate the cyclist's stopping distance.

phy_ocra.18.4.summary: A **large deceleration** means a vehicle (and the people in it) loses speed in a very short time, and by **force = mass x acceleration** this needs a very large force acting on the body, which can cause serious injury or death. Collisions are dangerous because the change in speed happens in a fraction of a second. Safety features such as **crumple zones, seat belts, airbags and helmets** work by **increasing the time** (and distance) over which a person stops, which **reduces the deceleration and therefore the force** for the same change in speed or momentum.

core.p: Newton's second law links force and acceleration. To slow a mass down, a resultant force must act opposite to its motion. The bigger the deceleration, the bigger that force must be.
bullets: **resultant force = mass x acceleration** (F = ma)
Deceleration is a negative acceleration: the velocity decreases
**acceleration = change in velocity / time** (a = Δv / t)
For the same change in speed, a shorter time means a larger deceleration
A larger deceleration of a person means a larger force on that person

callouts.p: The rate at which an object's velocity decreases (negative acceleration), measured in m/s².
Large deceleration -> large force (F = ma) -> risk of injury.

core.p: In a crash the car stops very suddenly. A person's body keeps moving forward because of its inertia until a force (from the seat belt, steering wheel, windscreen or road) stops it. If this happens in a very short time the force is huge.
bullets: A large force on the body can break bones and damage internal organs
The brain can hit the inside of the skull, causing head injury
The head can be thrown forward and back, causing **whiplash** neck injuries
Unrestrained passengers can hit the windscreen or be thrown from the car
Forces act on loose objects in the car too, which can hit occupants
The larger the speed before a crash, the larger the change in velocity and the greater the danger

callouts.t: Speed itself is not the danger
callouts.p: Moving at a steady high speed is not harmful. It is the large deceleration (rapid change of speed) that produces the dangerous force.

core.p: Normal braking produces small, safe decelerations. Collisions produce decelerations many times larger because the stopping time is so short.
bullets: Gentle braking in traffic: a few m/s²
Hard braking on a dry road: about 6 to 7 m/s²
Crash at 13 m/s stopping in 0.1 s: a = 13 / 0.1 = 130 m/s²
Same crash stopping in 0.02 s: a = 13 / 0.02 = 650 m/s²
Comparing with gravitational field strength (about 10 m/s²) helps: 130 m/s² is about 13 times g

core.h: Reducing the force by increasing time
core.p: In a collision the change in speed is fixed by how fast you were going. The only way to reduce the deceleration is to make the stop last longer.
bullets: a = Δv / t: **increasing t decreases a**
F = ma: **decreasing a decreases F**
Doubling the stopping time halves the deceleration and halves the force
This is the principle behind every passive safety feature

callouts.p: Feature -> increases the time taken to stop -> reduces deceleration -> reduces force on the person -> reduces injury. Write every link.

core.h: Reducing the force by increasing distance
core.p: The same idea can be explained with energy. The work done to stop a person equals their kinetic energy. Spreading the stop over a longer distance means a smaller force.
bullets: work done = force x distance = kinetic energy = 0.5 x m x v²
For the same kinetic energy, **larger stopping distance -> smaller force**
A crumple zone crushing by 0.5 m instead of 0.05 m reduces the average force by 10 times
An airbag lets the head travel further while slowing down

core.p: Force is also the rate of change of momentum. In a crash the change in momentum is fixed, so increasing the time reduces the force.
bullets: momentum = mass x velocity (p = mv), unit kg m/s
**force = change in momentum / time**
Change in momentum depends only on mass and change in velocity
Increase the time of the collision -> smaller rate of change of momentum -> smaller force
On a force-time graph the area under the graph equals the change in momentum; safety features make the graph lower and longer with the same area

callouts.p: Safety features do not reduce the change in momentum; they reduce the RATE of change of momentum.

core.p: Crumple zones are regions at the front and back of a car designed to crush in a controlled way during a collision.
bullets: They **deform** (crumple) on impact
This **increases the time** (and distance) over which the car, and the people in it, stop
So the **deceleration is smaller** and the **force on occupants is smaller**
Energy is transferred in doing work to deform the metal
The passenger compartment (**safety cell**) is rigid so it does not collapse onto occupants

callouts.p: Avoid saying the crumple zone 'absorbs the force' or 'absorbs the impact'. Say it increases the collision time, reducing deceleration and force; it absorbs energy by doing work deforming.

core.p: Seat belts hold occupants in their seats so they slow down with the car instead of continuing forward and hitting something hard.
bullets: The belt **stretches slightly**, increasing the time for the person to stop
So deceleration and force on the body are reduced
The force is **spread over a wider area** (chest and pelvis) so pressure is lower
Prevents the person hitting the windscreen, dashboard or being thrown out
Seat belts that have been in a crash should be replaced because they have been stretched

core.p: An airbag inflates rapidly in a crash, putting a soft cushion between the occupant and the steering wheel or dashboard.
bullets: The head and chest sink into the airbag, **increasing the stopping time and distance**
This reduces deceleration and the force on the head
The force is spread over a **larger area**, reducing pressure
Airbags work with seat belts; without a belt an occupant may hit the bag too hard

core.p: The same physics protects cyclists, motorcyclists and drivers outside the car.
bullets: **Cycle and motorcycle helmets**: a crushable foam layer increases the time for the head to stop, reducing force on the skull and brain; a hard shell spreads the force
**Crash barriers** on motorways bend, increasing the stopping time of a vehicle
**Gravel run-off areas** and sand traps stop vehicles over a longer distance
**Child car seats** hold small children so they decelerate with the car
Collapsible steering columns reduce force on the driver's chest

head: Feature
How it reduces force
rows: Cushions head; longer time, larger area
Foam crushes; longer time for head to stop
Bends; longer time for car to stop

core.p: You may need to estimate the force on a person in a crash, using typical masses and speeds.
bullets: Typical adult mass: about **70 kg**; typical car mass: about **1000 to 1500 kg**
Step 1: deceleration a = Δv / t
Step 2: force F = m x a
Example: 70 kg person, 13 m/s, stopped in 0.1 s: a = 130 m/s², F = 70 x 130 = 9100 N
Without a seat belt, hitting the dashboard in 0.01 s: a = 1300 m/s², F = 91 000 N

callouts.p: A 70 kg person weighs about 700 N. Comparing crash forces with body weight (e.g. 9100 N ≈ 13 x weight) shows how dangerous they are.

core.p: Questions may ask you to evaluate a feature or explain why speed limits matter.
bullets: Higher speed -> larger change in velocity in a crash -> larger deceleration and force
Kinetic energy ∝ v², so damage rises steeply with speed
Lower speed limits near schools reduce the forces in any collision with a pedestrian
Features add cost and mass to the car but greatly reduce injuries
Seat belts and airbags work best together

analogy.p: Catch a thrown egg with stiff hands and it stops in an instant: a huge deceleration, a huge force, a broken egg. Move your hands back with the egg as you catch it and it stops over a longer time and distance, so the force is small and it survives. Crumple zones, seat belts and airbags are the car's 'soft hands'. Where it breaks down: your hands can follow the egg for as long as you like, but a car only has a limited crumple length, and the safety cell must stay rigid to protect the people inside.

terms.d: Rate of decrease of velocity; negative acceleration, in m/s².
The single force with the same effect as all forces acting; F = ma.
The resultant force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.
The tendency of an object to keep moving at the same velocity unless a resultant force acts.
Mass x velocity, in kg m/s.
Change in momentum divided by time; equal to the resultant force.
Part of a car designed to crush in a collision, increasing collision time and reducing force on occupants.
The rigid passenger compartment that resists deforming in a crash.
A strap that stretches slightly to increase stopping time and spreads the force over the body.
A bag that inflates in a crash to increase the stopping time of the head and spread the force over a larger area.
Neck injury caused by the head being thrown forwards and backwards during a sudden deceleration.
The time over which the change of velocity happens in a crash.
0.5 x m x v²; energy that must be transferred when a moving object is stopped.
Force x distance; the energy transferred in stopping something.

mistakes.w: The crumple zone absorbs the force.
mistakes.r: The crumple zone increases the time of the collision, reducing the deceleration and so reducing the force (it absorbs energy by deforming).

mistakes.w: Seat belts reduce the momentum of the passenger.
mistakes.r: The change in momentum is the same; the seat belt increases the time so the rate of change of momentum (force) is smaller.

mistakes.w: Airbags make the collision time shorter.
mistakes.r: Airbags increase the time taken for the head to stop.

mistakes.w: Travelling at high speed causes injury.
mistakes.r: Injury is caused by large decelerations (rapid changes in speed), which need large forces.

mistakes.w: Increasing the time increases the deceleration.
mistakes.r: a = Δv / t, so a longer time gives a smaller deceleration.

mistakes.w: Safety features reduce the speed of the car.
mistakes.r: They do not change the change in speed; they spread it over a longer time.

mistakes.w: Force = mass / acceleration.
mistakes.r: Force = mass x acceleration.

mistakes.w: Helmets work because they are hard.
mistakes.r: The crushable lining increases the time for the head to stop, reducing the force; the hard shell spreads the force.

exam.q: State the equation that links resultant force, mass and acceleration.
model: force = mass x acceleration

exam.q: Explain why a large deceleration can injure a car passenger.
model: Large deceleration requires a large force (F = ma)
large force on the body causes injury

exam.q: A car travelling at 15 m/s crashes and stops in 0.1 s. Calculate its deceleration.
A 70 kg passenger decelerates at 150 m/s². Calculate the force on the passenger.
Explain how a seat belt reduces injuries in a crash.
model: Belt stretches, increasing the time for the passenger to stop
so deceleration is reduced
so force on the passenger is reduced (also spread over a larger area)
exam.tip: Every step of the chain earns a mark.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of momentum, how a crumple zone reduces the force on passengers. (Higher)
model: Change in momentum is the same
crumple zone increases the time of the collision
force = change in momentum / time, so force is smaller
exam.tip: Say the change in momentum is unchanged.

exam.q: A cycle helmet has a foam lining. Explain why this reduces head injuries.
model: Foam crushes, increasing the time taken for the head to stop
reducing the deceleration and so the force on the head
exam.tip: Talk about time, not 'absorbing the impact'.

exam.q: A crumple zone increases the collision time from 0.02 s to 0.1 s. By what factor is the force reduced?
model: Time increases by a factor of 5
force reduced by a factor of 5 (to one fifth)
exam.tip: F ∝ 1/t for the same change in velocity.

exam.q: Estimate the force on a 70 kg driver in a 30 mph crash if an airbag stops them in 0.2 s.
model: 30 mph ≈ 13 m/s

exam.q: Explain how the safety features of a modern car reduce the risk of injury to passengers in a collision. [6 marks]
model: In a crash a large deceleration needs a large force (F = ma), which causes injury
Crumple zones crush, increasing collision time
Seat belts stretch, increasing the time for the passenger to stop and spreading the force
Airbags increase the time and distance for the head to stop and spread the force over a larger area
Longer time means smaller deceleration (a = Δv/t) or smaller rate of change of momentum
so a smaller force on the passengers and less injury
exam.tip: Describe at least two features and give the full physics chain.

worked.q: A 75 kg motorcyclist travelling at 20 m/s hits a wall. Without a helmet the head stops in 0.005 s; the head has mass 5 kg. With a helmet it stops in 0.02 s. Compare the force on the head in each case.
steps: Time is 4 times longer, so force is 4 times smaller
worked.ans: 20 000 N without a helmet, 5000 N with a helmet (a quarter of the force)

worked.q: (Higher) A 1200 kg car travelling at 12 m/s stops in a crash. The crumple zone makes the collision last 0.15 s. Calculate the change in momentum and the average force.
steps: Change in momentum = m x Δv = 1200 x 12 = 14 400 kg m/s

worked.q: A 70 kg passenger moving at 13 m/s is stopped by a seat belt over a distance of 0.4 m. Estimate the average force on the passenger.
steps: Work done = force x distance, so F = 5915 / 0.4
If the passenger instead stopped in 0.04 m (hitting the dashboard), the force would be 10 times bigger, about 148 000 N
worked.ans: About 15 000 N (much smaller than without the belt)

phy_ocra.18.5.summary: Triple students must be able to **estimate the speeds, accelerations and forces** involved in everyday road situations such as a car pulling away, a lorry braking or a cyclist stopping. You combine **typical values** (masses, speeds and times you are expected to know) with the key equations **a = Δv / t**, **F = ma**, **v² - u² = 2as**, **work done = F x d** and, at Higher tier, **F = change in momentum / time**. Good estimates state their assumptions, use SI units, round sensibly and are checked against everyday experience.

core.p: Estimation questions do not give you every number. You must choose sensible typical values, use the correct equation and give a rounded answer of the right size.
bullets: Pick **typical values** and **state them** ('assume mass of car = 1000 kg')
Convert everything to **SI units**: kg, m, s, m/s, m/s², N
Use 1 or 2 significant figures in the final answer
Check the answer is sensible (a car's braking force is thousands of newtons, not millions)
There is often a range of acceptable answers

callouts.p: Examiners give marks for sensible assumed values and correct method, even if your number differs from the mark scheme's.

core.p: These are the values OCR expects you to be able to recall or judge.
bullets: Walking about **1.5 m/s**; running about 3 m/s; cycling about **6 m/s**
Car: about **13 m/s** in town (30 mph), **31 m/s** on a motorway (70 mph)
Speed of sound in air about 330 m/s (for comparison)
Mass of a person about **70 kg**; a car about **1000 to 1500 kg**; a large lorry up to about **40 000 kg**
Reaction time about 0.2 to 0.9 s
Car hard braking about 6 to 7 m/s²; car acceleration about 2 to 3 m/s²
g ≈ 10 N/kg (9.8 N/kg)

core.p: These equations from OCR's P1 to P2 content are used together in road problems.
bullets: **speed = distance / time** (v = d / t)
**acceleration = change in velocity / time** (a = Δv / t)
**force = mass x acceleration** (F = ma)
**(final velocity)² - (initial velocity)² = 2 x acceleration x distance** (data sheet)
**work done = force x distance**
**kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed²**
**momentum = mass x velocity** (p = mv)
**force = change in momentum / time** (Higher)
**power = work done / time**

head: To find
Use
Unit
rows: m x a, or Δp / t

core.p: Many road problems start with a speed in mph or km/h that must be changed to m/s.
bullets: km/h to m/s: **divide by 3.6** (e.g. 108 km/h = 30 m/s)
mph to m/s: multiply by about 0.45 (e.g. 30 mph ≈ 13 m/s)
Average speed of a journey = total distance / total time
A speed camera measures speed from distance between road markings and time between photos
Example: a car crosses two lines 5 m apart in 0.25 s: v = 5 / 0.25 = 20 m/s

callouts.p: Never use km/h or mph in F = ma or v² - u² = 2as. Convert to m/s first.

core.p: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken. If you know distance instead of time, use the data sheet equation.
bullets: a = (v - u) / t
Family car 0 to 27 m/s (60 mph) in about 10 s: a ≈ 2.7 m/s²
Bus pulling away: about 1 to 1.5 m/s²
Using distance: a = (v² - u²) / (2s)
A negative answer means deceleration

callouts.p: On a velocity-time graph, acceleration = gradient. A steeper line means a larger acceleration.

core.p: A journey graph lets you read off accelerations and distances directly.
bullets: **Gradient** = acceleration (positive when speeding up, negative when slowing down)
**Area under the graph** = distance travelled
Horizontal line = constant speed, so resultant force is zero
Split areas into rectangles and triangles
Steeper braking section = larger deceleration = larger braking force

core.p: Once you have an acceleration, Newton's second law gives the resultant force needed.
bullets: F = m x a: resultant force in newtons
Car 1000 kg accelerating at 2.5 m/s²: F = 2500 N resultant
Same car braking at 6.5 m/s²: braking force ≈ 6500 N
For the same force, a heavier vehicle has a smaller acceleration (a = F / m)
A loaded lorry needs a much larger force to give the same acceleration as a car

callouts.p: The resultant force on an object is equal to its mass multiplied by its acceleration.

core.p: A vehicle on the road has several forces acting on it. Its motion depends on the resultant force.
bullets: **Driving force** from the engine, via friction between tyres and road, acts forwards
**Resistive forces**: air resistance (drag) and friction act backwards
**Weight** acts downwards; the **normal contact force** of the road acts upwards and balances it
Driving force greater than resistive forces: resultant forwards, car accelerates
Driving force equals resistive forces: resultant zero, **constant speed** (top speed)
Air resistance increases with speed, so the acceleration gets smaller as the car speeds up

callouts.p: In F = ma, F is the RESULTANT force. If a car's engine gives 3000 N and resistive forces are 500 N, the resultant is 2500 N.

core.p: When braking, the work done by the braking force equals the kinetic energy of the vehicle.
bullets: F x d = 0.5 x m x v², so **F = 0.5 m v² / d**
Car 1000 kg at 13 m/s stopping in 13 m: F = 0.5 x 1000 x 169 / 13 = 6500 N
Larger speed: much larger force for the same distance (F ∝ v²)
Gives the same answer as F = ma with a from v² - u² = 2as

core.p: In collisions it is often easiest to use force as the rate of change of momentum.
bullets: p = mv; change in momentum = m x Δv
**F = Δp / t**
Car 1000 kg at 13 m/s stopping in 0.1 s: Δp = 13 000 kg m/s, F = 130 000 N
Increasing the collision time reduces the force
Momentum is conserved in a collision if no external forces act: total momentum before = total momentum after

callouts.p: F = Δp / t gives the same answer as F = m x (Δv / t); both are Newton's second law.

core.p: Estimates let you compare the physics of different vehicles and situations.
bullets: A lorry has about 40 times the mass of a car, so at the same speed about 40 times the kinetic energy and momentum
With a similar maximum braking force per kilogram, a loaded lorry needs a large braking force to stop
A cyclist (about 80 kg with bike) at 6 m/s has a kinetic energy of about 1400 J; a car at 13 m/s about 85 000 J
Pedestrians are hurt much more by a car at 30 mph than at 20 mph because KE ∝ v²

core.p: A grade 9 answer always sanity-checks the result.
bullets: Is the order of magnitude right? Braking forces on cars are about 10³ to 10⁴ N
Collision forces are much larger: about 10⁴ to 10⁵ N
Compare with weight: a 1000 kg car weighs about 10 000 N
Accelerations bigger than about 10 m/s² are unusual for normal driving
If the answer is silly, look for a units slip (mph, km/h, g instead of kg)

callouts.p: Keep full figures in working; round only the final answer to 1 or 2 significant figures.

analogy.p: Estimating is like cooking from a recipe when you do not have scales: you know a 'cupful' and a 'spoonful' (typical speeds, masses and times) and the method (the equations) and you still get a sensible cake. Different cooks get slightly different cakes, just as different students choose slightly different values, but all should be recognisably cakes, the right order of magnitude. Where it breaks down: a recipe works with any ingredients, but in physics your typical values must be realistic or the answer is wrong by orders of magnitude.

terms.d: An approximate answer found using sensible typical values and rounding.
A realistic everyday value, e.g. car mass 1000 kg, town speed 13 m/s.
Distance travelled per unit time; a scalar, in m/s.
Speed in a given direction; a vector, in m/s.
Change in velocity divided by time taken, in m/s².
Negative acceleration; rate at which velocity decreases.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
The forward force on a vehicle from the engine, acting through friction between tyres and road.

mistakes.w: Using the engine force instead of the resultant force in F = ma.
mistakes.r: F is the resultant force: driving force minus resistive forces.

mistakes.w: Using speed in km/h or mph in the equations.
mistakes.r: Convert to m/s first (divide km/h by 3.6).

mistakes.w: Choosing a car mass of 100 kg or 100 000 kg.
mistakes.r: A typical car is about 1000 to 1500 kg.

mistakes.w: a = v / t with v as the final speed when the car did not start from rest.
mistakes.r: a = (v - u) / t uses the CHANGE in velocity.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to square the speed in v² - u² = 2as or KE.
mistakes.r: Square the speed: KE = 0.5 x m x v².

mistakes.w: A car at constant speed has no forces acting on it.
mistakes.r: The forces are balanced: driving force equals resistive forces, so the resultant is zero.

mistakes.w: Mixing up mass and weight (using 10 000 for a 1000 kg car in F = ma).
mistakes.r: Use mass in kg in F = ma; weight (N) = mass x g.

mistakes.w: Giving a long unrounded estimate such as 6538.46 N.
mistakes.r: Round to a sensible 1 or 2 significant figures, e.g. about 6500 N.

model: v² - u² = 2as: 0 - 30² = 2 x a x 75
deceleration = 6 m/s²

exam.q: (Higher) A 1500 kg car travelling at 14 m/s hits a barrier and stops in 0.2 s. Calculate the average force on the car.
Explain why a car's acceleration decreases as its speed increases, even when the driving force stays the same.
model: Air resistance increases with speed
so the resultant force (driving minus resistive) decreases
so acceleration (a = F/m) decreases, reaching zero at top speed

exam.q: A lorry and a car both travel at 25 m/s. Use estimates to explain why the lorry needs a much larger braking force to stop in the same distance. [6 marks]
model: Typical car mass about 1000 kg, lorry about 40 000 kg
Same speed and distance so same deceleration needed: a = 25² / (2 x d)
F = ma, so force ∝ mass
Lorry needs about 40 times the braking force of the car
Or: lorry KE = 0.5 x 40 000 x 625 ≈ 12.5 MJ versus about 0.3 MJ for the car
Work done = F x d, so with the same distance the lorry needs a much larger force
exam.tip: Give numbers for both vehicles and compare them.
